parts.title: Riding with Bella
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
I was ten when I first sat on a horse. My aunt owned a small farm, and she had an old brown mare called Bella. I was terrified. Bella seemed as big as a house, and I was sure that she did not like me.

My aunt laughed and said that horses can feel when you are afraid. She told me to breathe slowly and to stroke Bella's neck. After a few minutes, my hands stopped shaking, and Bella made a soft noise. My aunt said that it meant "hello".

That summer, I rode every day. I learnt to walk, then to trot, and at the end of August, I managed to gallop across a field. I felt like I was flying. One afternoon, Bella stopped suddenly, and I fell off into the grass. I was not hurt, but I cried. My aunt said, "Every rider falls off. The important thing is to get back on."

So I did. Now, twenty years later, I still ride every weekend, and I often think of Bella. She taught me that being brave is not the same as not being afraid.

questions.explanation: She was terrified.

questions.explanation: Her aunt told her to breathe slowly and stroke Bella's neck.

questions.explanation: Her aunt said it meant "hello".

questions.explanation: Being brave is not the same as not being afraid.

parts.title: Horses in history
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
Horses have lived beside people for about six thousand years. [1] The first people to ride them probably lived on the grasslands of Central Asia.

At first, horses were used for food, but later, people discovered how strong they were. [2] A horse could pull a plough, a cart or even a heavy gun.

In battles, soldiers on horseback could move much faster than soldiers on foot. [3] For hundreds of years, armies depended on horses to carry messages and supplies.

On farms, horses worked hard until the twentieth century. [4] When tractors arrived, the number of working horses fell quickly.

Today, horses are mainly kept for sport and pleasure. [5] There are thousands of riding clubs around the world, and many people say that a horse is the best friend they have ever had.
sentences: Cats and dogs were kept in houses.
Nobody is sure exactly when this began.
Their strong backs and legs made them useful for many jobs.
This gave their owners a great advantage.
My uncle trains them every morning before breakfast.
Donkeys and camels were more useful in dry countries.
They are no longer needed for heavy work.

gaps.explanation: Nobody is sure when it began; the next sentence mentions the first riders.
Their strong backs and legs made them useful; the next sentence gives jobs such as pulling a plough.
This gave their owners a great advantage; the next sentence says armies depended on horses.
Then things began to change; the next sentence says what happened when tractors arrived.
Horses are no longer needed for heavy work; the next sentence says there are riding clubs.

parts.title: Looking after a horse
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: Owning a horse is a big job. A horse needs food, water and exercise every day, [1] when the weather is bad. Every morning, someone must check [2] the animal looks well and is walking normally. The stable should be cleaned daily, and the bedding must be dry. Horses are social animals, [3] they do not like to be alone. Many owners keep two horses together, or a horse and a goat. Brushing is also important. It keeps the coat clean and [4] the owner a chance to look for cuts and sore places. A horse also needs a visit from the vet at least [5] a year. Finally, remember that horses can live for thirty years, so you should be sure that you can look after one for a [6] time before you buy it.

gaps.explanation: Even when the weather is bad: emphasis.
Check that the animal looks well.
Social animals, so they do not like to be alone.
Brushing gives the owner a chance.
At least once a year: frequency.
The adjective long describes the time: a long time.

parts.title: A message about a horse show
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: organiser
turns.text: Hello, everybody. This is Jem, the organiser of the Greenfield Horse Show. This is the twentieth year of the show, and we expect more than three thousand visitors. I would like to give you the final details. Please write down the important times, because there will be no printed programme. The show takes place on Sunday the ninth of August, and the gates open at eight in the morning. The early visitors can see the horses arrive and watch the riders prepare. The first event is the children's pony race at ten o'clock. Children from six to twelve can take part, and every child receives a ribbon. After that, there will be a jumping competition, which begins at noon. Some of the best riders in the country will take part, and the fences are one metre forty high. The grand parade, with more than forty horses, will start at three. Each horse has a flower on its head, and the riders wear traditional clothes. We have a special area for picnics, and the cafe will sell hot food all day. You can also bring your own sandwiches, but please do not leave any rubbish. Parking is free, but please do not park near the main gate. Instead, use the big field behind the church, and a bus will take you to the entrance. We also need volunteers to help with the stands. You will sell tickets, give out programmes or help with the food, and you will get a free lunch. If you can help, please phone me before Friday. The telephone number is on the poster. See you all there!

gaps.prompt: The show is on Sunday the ___ of August
gaps.explanation: He says the show is on Sunday the ninth of August.

gaps.prompt: The gates open at ___ in the morning
gaps.explanation: He says the gates open at eight.

gaps.prompt: The children's pony race begins at ___ o'clock
gaps.explanation: He says it is at ten o'clock.

gaps.prompt: The grand parade has more than ___ horses
gaps.explanation: He says more than forty horses.
He says to phone before Friday.

parts.title: An interview with a jockey
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Pace, you are a professional jockey. How did you begin?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: My parents have a stable. I sat on a pony before I could walk, and by ten I was competing in local races.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Did you go to school normally?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Yes, but I did my homework in the stable. My teachers were very kind, and one of them even came to watch my first big race.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Is it dangerous?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Yes. I have broken my collarbone twice and my wrist once. But I wear a helmet and a special jacket, and my team looks after me well.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What do your parents say about the dangers?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: They worry, of course. My mother checks my helmet every morning, and my father calls me after each race.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: How do you recover after an injury?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Slowly. First I rest, then I swim, and then I ride a quiet horse. The worst part is watching races on television while I wait.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Do you have to be small?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Light, rather than small. I weigh fifty kilos, so I have to be careful about what I eat. Often, I have a salad when everyone else has a pizza.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: How do you travel to races?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: In a lorry with the horses, sometimes for six hours. I sleep in the back, on a pile of blankets, and the horses seem to like the company.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Do you ever feel hungry?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: All the time! But I have learned that a small meal, eaten slowly, can be very satisfying. After a race, I eat as much as I want, and my mother cooks my favourite dish.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: How do you get on with the horses?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Very close. I visit them early every morning, before breakfast. They know my voice and seem to know when I am nervous.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Which horse do you love most?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: A grey one called Mist. She is small but very brave, and she once won a race by a nose. When I whisper to her, she moves her ears.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What is the best moment of a race?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: The final hundred metres, when the horse and I are completely together. It is like music.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What do you think about before a race?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: I think about my breathing and about the first turn. I try to be calm, because horses feel what we feel.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What would you do if you stopped racing?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: I would become a trainer. I love teaching young riders, because they remind me of myself.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Do you have a message for young riders?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Be patient and kind to your horse. A good rider listens to the horse, not only gives orders.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Thank you, Pace, and good luck on Saturday.

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Thank you. I will do my best, and so will Mist.
